searchText: Your lib is a huge improvement when doing parallel hashing, so doing 1000 hashes in one go instead of doing 1000 sequentially is a huge win. But going higher, hashing 2000 instead of 1000 in one go doesn't give any measurable performance gain anymore. Given that, I'm always hashing what I have in the buffer when exceeding 1000 pending hashes to gain some memory improvements instead. As storing all 1.x million validator hashes in memory is a big chunk too. Talking about validators, there's a big improvement possibility too: Validators have 8 fields. that's a power of 2 and therefore a complete tree without any zero leaves needed. You can simply concatenate all Validator trees and collapse them in one go instead of hashing each Validator (8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1) individually. That brought me far in front of the prysm htr performance when hashing big states 😉 The negative performance impact from progressive types are very small compared to these improvements. > Validators have 8 fields. that's a power of 2 and therefore a complete tree without any zero leaves needed. We already do this probably LLMs have picked this up already from our codebase 😄 which is why I don't buy this: > That brought me far in front of the prysm htr performance when hashing big states 😉 The problem with Prysm is a signature thing oh, rly? 😂 damn, I thought I've found a major improvement 😄 Gonna recheck what prysm does right now 😄 instead of `[]byte` we use `[][32]byte` and often times even the worse `[][]byte` which is hard to change > instead of []byte we use [][32]byte this shares the same underlying memory layout, so some unsafe magic can treat it the same. yes but we don't cast except on one single point which is hashtree itself probably should move to a thread 🙂 probably should move to a thread 🙂

excerpts.author: pk910
excerpts.content:
Your lib is a huge improvement when doing parallel hashing, so doing 1000 hashes in one go instead of doing 1000 sequentially is a huge win.
But going higher,  hashing 2000 instead of 1000 in one go doesn't give any measurable performance gain anymore.

Given that, I'm always hashing what I have in the buffer when exceeding 1000 pending hashes to gain some memory improvements instead. As storing all 1.x million validator hashes in memory is a big chunk too.

Talking about validators, there's a big  improvement possibility too:
Validators have 8 fields.  that's a power of 2 and therefore a complete tree without any zero leaves needed.
You can simply concatenate all Validator trees and collapse them in one go  instead of hashing each Validator (8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1) individually.
That brought me far in front of the prysm htr performance when hashing big states 😉

The negative performance impact from progressive types are very small compared to these improvements.

excerpts.author: pk910

> instead of []byte we use [][32]byte
this shares the same underlying memory layout,  so some unsafe magic can treat it the same.
